name: Laryngoplasty / Adam's apple surgery
lead: Chondrolaryngoplasty, popularly called a tracheal shave, reduces the thyroid cartilage that forms the Adam's apple, the bump at the front of the neck. People have it done to flatten the neck profile so the throat looks smoother and, for many, more feminine. The nickname is a misnomer because the trachea is not involved.[1]

The Adam's apple is the laryngeal prominence, the angle of the thyroid cartilage around the larynx. It is usually much more noticeable in adult men, where cartilage growth and forward movement during puberty, driven mainly by testosterone, make it stand out; in women it sits higher and is often small.[2] Chondrolaryngoplasty is among the more common procedures for transgender women and is also sought by others who want a less prominent Adam's apple for aesthetic reasons.[1][3]

The operation was first described by Francis G. Wolfort and Richard G. Parry in 1975. The voice is usually unaffected, though slight pitch changes have been reported, and most patients are satisfied.[1] Surgical reviews describe it as commonly done as part of facial feminization surgery and emphasise preserving laryngeal integrity while reducing the prominence.[3][4]

paras: In the standard approach a surgeon makes a small horizontal incision, often in a skin fold at the base of the Adam's apple, and shaves the cartilage with a scalpel under local or general anesthesia. Newer variants place the incision under the chin or inside the mouth and may be done endoscopically.[1]

Surgical reviews describe visualising the vocal cords with flexible laryngoscopy and using intraoperative needle localisation of the anterior commissure to guide how much cartilage is removed, which is intended to protect voice outcomes.[3][4] The procedure can be combined with other facial feminization surgeries.[3]

Swelling, bruising and difficulty swallowing or speaking are common to varying degrees. The red incision line lasts about six weeks and full recovery averages about two weeks; many surgeons recommend rubbing the incision to limit visible scarring.[1]

Because the vocal folds lie close to the site, they can rarely be damaged, and slight pitch changes have been reported.[1] Most patients are satisfied; the usual complaints are that the Adam's apple still looks too large or that the scar is noticeable.[1] Wikipedia notes feminization laryngoplasty, a more complex procedure that also alters the vocal cords, can address insufficient reduction but changes the voice and carries more risk.[1][2]

A different group of operations changes the voice rather than the cartilage shape. Pitch-reduction thyroplasty is described in a review as being used mainly in transgender men who do not get enough pitch reduction from speech therapy and masculinising hormone therapy.[5] Some transgender men also seek to enlarge the prominence, and testosterone can enlarge the larynx.[2]

No studies found in a dedicated trial sense; the evidence consists of surgical technique reviews of chondrolaryngoplasty[3][4] and the satisfaction and systematic-review literature cited in Wikipedia's account of the procedure.[1]

card.summary: Surgery that shaves down the Adam's apple; usually satisfied patients, rare vocal fold risk.
card.note: Surgical risks include rare vocal fold injury; no formal studies were reviewed.

quick.overview:
This surgery trims the thyroid cartilage to flatten a prominent Adam's apple. It is common in gender-affirming care and also used cosmetically.

Wikipedia reports most patients are satisfied; complaints concern residual prominence or scarring.
quick.mechanism: A surgeon makes a small incision and shaves the cartilage, sometimes endoscopically through the chin or mouth.
quick.risks: The vocal folds are close, so rare damage and slight pitch changes are reported. Swelling, bruising and temporary swallowing difficulty are common during about two weeks of recovery.

chain: Surgeon reduces the thyroid cartilage prominence
A smoother, less angular throat line
angle.text: The procedure removes part of the cartilage that creates the visible bump, changing the neck profile directly. People seek it for a smoother throat, often alongside other facial feminization procedures.
